newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus standoff pits president against the rest.
newsitem.headline: Belarus standoff pits president against the rest.

text.p: Here is an outline of leading issues, individuals and rival institutions in Belarus, where President Alexander Lukashenko is trying to increase his powers in a referendum on November 24.

THE PRESIDENT - Alexander Lukashenko, a 42-year-old former state farm chief and political instructor in the Soviet army who won the presidency by a landslide in July 1994, promising to fight corruption and create some form of union with Russia.
He is seeking to recommence his five-year term through the referendum, extending it to November 2001, and increase his authority over parliament and other institutions.

THE PRIME MINISTER - Mikhail Chigir, a former banker appointed soon after the 1994 election by Lukashenko. Seen as a professional and well-respected in the former Soviet republic of 10 million, he dealt a blow to Lukashenko by threatening to resign on Monday unless Lukashenko dropped the referendum.

PARLIAMENT - Elected in 1995, communist, liberal and nationalist deputies have joined forces, creating a majority big enough to oppose Lukashenko who ignores their decisions and those of the constitutional court. A single group of about 60 deputies backs the president. Around 100 Communists and Agrarians and around 35 liberals and social democrats oppose him, saying he is building a dictatorship. Only 199 out of a possible 260 seats were filled at the elections.
Backed by the constitutional court, they voted that the referendum should be advisory rather than carrying legal force, but Lukashenko overturned their decision by decree.
Deputies on Monday were seeking to impeach the president, for which they would need a two-thirds majority.

THE CONSTITUTIONAL COURT - Like parliament, a majority of 11 judges oppose Lukashenko. The court has issued rulings against 17 presidential decrees which he has ignored. He overturned by decree their decision that the referendum should be advisory.

THE CENTRAL COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS AND REFERENDUMS - A panel of 13 people who monitor and organise the elections. Under Viktor Gonchar, sacked by Lukashenko on November 14 though he is appointed by parliament. Nine of the 13 have signed a letter supporting Gonchar's sacking.

THE CONSTITUTION - Passed by deputies -- and co-written by Lukashenko -- in April 1994, the president has since dismissed the constitution as inadequate. His opponents say presidential decrees muzzling the media and overturning court decisions violate the 1994 constitution.

THE MEDIA - State television is under the control of the president, allowing him unlimited access to the airwaves and opposition figures none. One other commercial Belarussian television also runs mainly entertainment programmes for a few hours a night. Lukashenko closed the country's single independent radio station. His Security Council has also threatened to block transmission of one of four Russian channels, NTV, accusing it of trying to block the referendum.

THE PEOPLE - They are impoverished, ill-informed and in the provinces convinced that Lukashenko is a hero struggling against an evil opposition. About 40 percent said they would back him in the referendum in an independent opinion poll a month ago. He would need the backing of 50 percent of the electorate, plus one vote, to win the referendum. Two thirds would have to take part in voting.
